package.title: The AI Bubble Is Real. What Survives Is Steel.
package.promised: A grounded look at whether the AI investment bubble is real, and why physical infrastructure like steel may outlast speculative hype. I expect to learn what parts of the AI boom are durable and what signals point to a bust.

new_things: The safest thing you own is compared to an iron spike.
The iron spike ruined almost everyone who touched it.
The year associated with the spike was 1845.
Someone today is watching his fourth version of the same chart during his lunch break.
The chart is being presented in different voices.
reports.held_question: What is the chart about, and how does it connect to the iron spike and the AI investment bubble?
could_not_follow: The sentence ending with “Different voice” was incomplete.

new_things: The chart has two lines.
AI is being compared to 1845 again.
The chart is repeatedly copied, with each version becoming louder.
The people who built it are usually not named.
No one checked the original chart's math.
Index funds are already holding something related to it, but the sentence was cut off.
reports.held_question: What is the index fund already holding?
could_not_follow: What exactly AI is being compared to in 1845

new_things: The original chart comes from Bravos Research.
It is described as a sharp macro chart on YouTube.
The chart compares two lines involving mega-cap companies: Meta, Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, and Alphabet.
reports.held_question: What do the chart’s two lines show, and how do they support the claim that AI is 1845 again?

new_things: The mega-caps rose 21% in a year.
The index was plotted beneath them and followed the same line.
The giants now represent the market.
The chip industry rose 105% and outpaced both the giants and the index.
Bravos’ chart left out another layer.
reports.held_question: What is the layer that Bravos’ chart never drew?

The chart is considered correct, but its warning is aimed at the wrong place.
What follows will be one test, not a rebuttal, victory lap, or panic.

It should take about thirty seconds to run the test on each stock.
The opponent is the hype cycle, a machine that attracts capital.

The example begins with railways.

It counts computing and software as a share of private investment.
At the dot-com peak, computing and software made up 23 cents of every private investment dollar.
Today that share is 28 cents, the highest ever.

new_things: In 1849, the thing that lasted was the steel rather than the paper.
The trains kept running through the crash, and towns continued growing around their stations.
The steel kept functioning while the paper stopped pretending.
The question now is who is paying for the steel.
For years, the giants paid for all of it.

could_not_follow: The sentence about the giants paying for all of it is unfinished.

new_things: For years, the giants funded everything from cash on hand without borrowing.
Their bills eventually became larger than their cash reserves.
From 2020 to 2024, the biggest builders borrowed about $28 billion per year.
Last year, they borrowed $121 billion.
This year’s borrowing is expected to be even higher.
reports.held_question: How much are they tracking toward borrowing this year?
could_not_follow: The sentence cuts off before giving this year’s figure.

new_things: The builders are on track to borrow $150 billion this year.
That level of borrowing could significantly affect the bond market.
Technology now makes up about 10% of the investment-grade bond index, up from about 9%.
Technology's share is projected to rise above 12%.
reports.held_question: Where did the money used to sit, and where is it moving now?

new_things: Money in utilities and banks is becoming a bet on data centers.
Data-center spending is not slowing down.
The spending estimate rose from $480 billion to $690 billion.
The estimate increased faster than the year progressed.
There are another $822 billion in lease commitments.
These are for data centers already contracted and agreed to be paid for.
Those lease commitments have not appeared on balance sheets.

new_things: The buildout consumes all of the companies’ operating cash, so they are borrowing to cover the difference.
The buildout used to be funded from profits, but that stopped about eighteen months ago.
Nobody involved committed fraud.
They signed a promise during a good year.
The physical buildout continued while the paperwork and obligations grew heavier.

new_things: The bubble is in the financial paper around the steel infrastructure, not in AI stocks.
The 1845 crisis in England was caused by railway certificates rather than railways themselves.
reports.held_question: How did railway certificates break England in 1845?

new_things: The paper promises were priced using the best year and held by people who had not checked what they owned.
Bravos has a number showing where that paper exists today.
AI builders make up 20% of the S&P 500, compared with a historical 2–4%.

new_things: Every index fund has about one-fifth of its value tied to AI companies.
Target-date funds also have that same exposure and are commonly the default retirement option.
If the AI companies lose half their value, the overall market would drop about 10%.
reports.asked_of_me: Calculate the market impact if AI stocks fall by half.

new_things: The other 490 companies effectively have no say in the market’s movement.
The real risk was the certificates representing ownership, not the price spike itself.
A bubble happens when ownership grows faster than people’s understanding, rather than when the technology fails.
In 1845, the railway infrastructure worked, but railway investments still lost about two-thirds of their value.
Railway steel remained unused for twenty years while the economy caught up.
The eventual return took two decades.
reports.held_question: What does 1845 prove, and what step is missing from the railway map?
could_not_follow: The jump to 1845 and what it refers to.
Why working railway infrastructure still led to a two-thirds loss.

new_things: Today's compute depreciates in about five years.

new_things: The builders have a deeper moat than paper holders can see.

new_things: The test has three questions: whether what a holding sells is scarce or abundant, whether its growth is funded by earned cash or issued paper, and whether it would still be used if hype disappeared.
Scarcity can be recognized through being sold out, becoming more expensive, or being fought over.
reports.held_question: How would a particular holding perform when judged by these three questions?
reports.asked_of_me: Take any holding and ask it these three questions.

new_things: You can check all three questions from your phone.
Scarcity appears in order-book signals such as sellouts, waitlists, and rising prices.
A finance site shows the cash answer through operating cash flow and the share count.
reports.held_question: What is the significance if cash flow is positive?

new_things: Positive operating cash flow and a stable share count mean the company is not issuing shares to survive.
You can test an asset by imagining whether it would still be used without hype.
Steel is presented as scarce, cash-generating, and useful.
Paper is presented as abundant, issued, and dependent on belief.
